subject: Government
title: Nationalism and Independence
outline: Meaning, causes and phases of Nigerian nationalism
Nationalist movements, parties and the nationalist press
The road to independence and the First Republic
Military rule in Nigeria: causes, features, merits and demerits

modules.title: Module 1: Nationalism and the Struggle for Independence
modules.html:
Nationalism is the desire and organised effort of a people with common history, culture and aspirations to free themselves from foreign domination and govern themselves.

Causes of Nigerian Nationalism

  1. Racial discrimination and exclusion of Africans from senior posts in the colonial service.
  2. Economic exploitation — expatriate control of trade, low producer prices, forced labour and taxation.
  3. Western education, which produced an elite exposed to ideas of liberty, equality and self-determination.
  4. Influence of returnee ex-servicemen from the Second World War, who had fought for freedom abroad.
  5. The Atlantic Charter (1941), in which Churchill and Roosevelt affirmed the right of peoples to choose their own government.
  6. Pan-Africanism and the Diaspora — W.E.B. Du Bois, Marcus Garvey and the Pan-African Congresses.
  7. Independence of other countries — India (1947), Ghana (1957).
  8. The nationalist press — Azikiwe's West African Pilot, Macaulay's Lagos Daily News.
  9. Activities of the United Nations and its anti-colonial resolutions.

Nationalist Organisations

OrganisationYearLeader(s)
Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP)1923Herbert Macaulay
Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM)1934/1936Ernest Ikoli, H.O. Davies, Samuel Akinsanya, Obafemi Awolowo
National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC)1944Herbert Macaulay and Nnamdi Azikiwe
Action Group (AG)1951Obafemi Awolowo (from Egbe Omo Oduduwa)
Northern People's Congress (NPC)1951Ahmadu Bello, Abubakar Tafawa Balewa (from Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa)
Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU)1950Aminu Kano

Leading Nationalists

  • Herbert Macaulay — "father of Nigerian nationalism"; founded the NNDP and used the press to attack colonial injustice.
  • Nnamdi Azikiwe — founded the West African Pilot, led the NCNC, became first indigenous Governor-General and first President.
  • Obafemi Awolowo — led the AG and the Western Region; pioneered free primary education, free health care and television in Africa.
  • Ahmadu Bello — Sardauna of Sokoto, Premier of the North, leader of the NPC.
  • Abubakar Tafawa Balewa — first and only Prime Minister of Nigeria.
  • Aminu Kano, Anthony Enahoro (who moved the 1953 self-government motion), Margaret Ekpo, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti and Hajia Gambo Sawaba — other prominent nationalists.

The Road to Independence

Constitutional conferences in London and Lagos (1953, 1954, 1957, 1958) fixed the terms of independence. The West and East became self-governing in 1957, the North in 1959. Federal elections in December 1959 produced an NPC–NCNC coalition, and Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960, with Balewa as Prime Minister and Azikiwe as Governor-General.

examples.q: How did the Second World War accelerate nationalism in Nigeria?
examples.a: Nigerian ex-servicemen fought alongside Europeans in Burma and East Africa, discovered that colonial rulers were not invincible, and returned expecting jobs and rights. The Atlantic Charter of 1941 proclaimed the right of all peoples to choose their government, which nationalists quoted against Britain. The war also weakened Britain economically, strengthened anti-colonial opinion internationally, and disrupted colonial trade, which sharpened economic grievances at home.

examples.q: Assess the role of the press in the nationalist struggle.
examples.a: Newspapers such as Macaulay's Lagos Daily News and Azikiwe's West African Pilot exposed colonial injustice, educated and mobilised the public, publicised party programmes, and created a national audience beyond ethnic boundaries. They trained a generation of politically conscious readers and gave nationalist leaders a platform that the colonial government could not easily silence, making the press one of the most effective weapons of the struggle.

modules.title: Module 2: The First Republic and Its Collapse
modules.html:
The First Republic (1963–1966) operated a parliamentary system with four regions. It collapsed under the weight of accumulated crises.

Crises of the First Republic

  1. 1962/63 census controversy — inflated figures because population determined revenue and parliamentary seats.
  2. Action Group crisis (1962) — the Awolowo–Akintola split, a state of emergency in the West and the treasonable felony trial.
  3. Creation of the Mid-West Region (1963) — seen as a partisan move against the AG.
  4. 1964 federal election crisis — boycott by the UPGA and a constitutional stand-off between Azikiwe and Balewa.
  5. 1965 Western Region election — massive rigging and the "Operation Wetie" violence.
  6. Ethnic and regional politics, corruption and nepotism throughout.

On 15 January 1966 a group of majors led by Chukwuma Kaduna Nzeogwu staged Nigeria's first coup, killing Balewa, Ahmadu Bello and Akintola. Major-General J.T.U. Aguiyi-Ironsi assumed power and promulgated Decree No. 34 of 1966, abolishing the federation and creating a unitary state. A counter-coup in July 1966 brought Lt-Col Yakubu Gowon to power; pogroms and the failure of the Aburi Accord led to the declaration of Biafra and the civil war of 1967–1970.

examples.q: Why did Decree No. 34 of 1966 provoke such strong opposition?
examples.a: It abolished the federal structure and the regions, replacing them with a unitary state with provinces, and unified the public service. Northerners feared that a single national civil service would allow better-educated southerners to dominate appointments, and the decree was interpreted as confirming that the January coup was an Igbo plot to dominate Nigeria. The resulting suspicion contributed directly to the counter-coup of July 1966 and the killings that followed.

examples.q: Explain two ways the census controversy destabilised the First Republic.
examples.a: First, population figures determined the sharing of federal revenue and the allocation of parliamentary seats, so inflated returns gave a region political and financial advantage, provoking bitter accusations of fraud. Second, the dispute hardened regional mistrust between North and South and undermined confidence in federal institutions, making peaceful competition for power increasingly difficult.

modules.title: Module 3: Military Rule in Nigeria
modules.html:
A military government is one in which the armed forces seize and exercise political power, usually after a coup d'etat, ruling by decree rather than by constitution.

Causes of Military Intervention

  1. Corruption and mismanagement by politicians
  2. Electoral malpractice and violence
  3. Ethnicity, nepotism and regionalism
  4. Economic mismanagement and decline
  5. Personal ambition of officers and indiscipline in the army
  6. Weak institutions and loss of legitimacy of civilian rulers
  7. The demonstration effect of coups elsewhere in Africa

Features of Military Rule

  • Suspension or modification of parts of the constitution
  • Rule by decree; decrees are supreme and often protected by ouster clauses
  • Abolition of the legislature and political parties; fusion of executive and legislative powers in the Supreme Military Council
  • Centralisation of power and a chain-of-command hierarchy
  • Restriction of fundamental rights and press freedom
  • The judiciary survives but with limited jurisdiction; military tribunals try many offences

Timeline of Regimes

PeriodHead of GovernmentNote
Jan–Jul 1966Aguiyi-IronsiDecree No. 34; unitary experiment
1966–1975Yakubu GowonCivil war; 12 states created in 1967
1975–1976Murtala MohammedPurge of the public service; 19 states; FCT Abuja
1976–1979Olusegun ObasanjoLocal government reform; handover in 1979
1979–1983Shehu ShagariSecond Republic (civilian)
1983–1985Muhammadu BuhariWar Against Indiscipline
1985–1993Ibrahim BabangidaSAP; two-party system; annulment of 12 June 1993
1993Ernest ShonekanInterim National Government
1993–1998Sani AbachaRepression; six geo-political zones concept
1998–1999Abdulsalami AbubakarTransition to the Fourth Republic

Merits and Demerits

Merits: quick decision-making, restoration of order after breakdown, creation of states and local government reform, nationwide programmes such as the NYSC (1973), UPE and WAI. Demerits: dictatorship and abuse of human rights, absence of accountability and the rule of law, corruption, politicisation of the army, discouragement of foreign investment, and destruction of democratic institutions.

examples.q: Distinguish between a coup d'etat and a revolution.
examples.a: A coup d'etat is a sudden, usually violent seizure of governmental power by a small group, typically military officers, which changes the personnel of government but leaves the social and economic structure largely intact. A revolution is a fundamental, often mass-based transformation of the entire political, social and economic order, as in France in 1789 or Russia in 1917. Nigeria's 1966 event was a coup, not a revolution.

examples.q: State three positive contributions of military regimes in Nigeria.
examples.a: First, the creation of states, from 12 in 1967 to 36 by 1996, addressed minority demands and brought administration closer to the people. Second, the 1976 local government reform standardised the third tier nationwide and gave it direct funding. Third, national integration schemes such as the National Youth Service Corps (1973) and the establishment of the Federal Capital Territory at Abuja promoted unity.

quiz.q: Herbert Macaulay is regarded as the father of Nigerian nationalism because he
options: Founded the NNDP and pioneered nationalist agitation
quiz.solution: Macaulay founded the first Nigerian political party in 1923 and used the press against colonial injustice.

quiz.q: The West African Pilot was founded by
quiz.solution: Azikiwe established the West African Pilot in 1937 as a nationalist newspaper.

quiz.q: The motion for self-government in 1956 was moved in 1953 by
quiz.solution: Chief Anthony Enahoro of the Action Group moved the historic self-government motion.

quiz.q: Which document proclaimed the right of all peoples to choose their form of government and inspired nationalists?
quiz.solution: The 1941 Atlantic Charter was widely cited by African nationalists demanding self-determination.

quiz.q: The NCNC was formed in 1944 under the leadership of
quiz.solution: Herbert Macaulay was president and Nnamdi Azikiwe secretary of the NCNC.

quiz.q: The Action Group grew out of the cultural organisation known as
quiz.solution: Awolowo transformed the Yoruba cultural group Egbe Omo Oduduwa into the Action Group in 1951.

quiz.q: Nigeria's first military coup took place on
quiz.solution: The Nzeogwu-led coup of 15 January 1966 ended the First Republic.

quiz.q: Decree No. 34 of 1966 is remembered for
options: Abolishing the federal system and imposing a unitary state
quiz.solution: Ironsi's Unification Decree replaced the federation with a unitary state, provoking widespread opposition.

quiz.q: Twelve states were created in Nigeria in 1967 by
quiz.solution: General Gowon created 12 states on the eve of the civil war to weaken secessionist support.

quiz.q: The National Youth Service Corps was established in
quiz.solution: The NYSC was created in 1973 to promote national integration after the civil war.

quiz.q: A key feature of military rule is
quiz.solution: Military regimes legislate by decree, which is superior to other laws and often shielded by ouster clauses.

quiz.q: The annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election was carried out by the regime of
quiz.solution: General Ibrahim Babangida annulled the June 12, 1993 election won by M.K.O. Abiola.

quiz.q: The War Against Indiscipline was launched by
quiz.solution: WAI was a hallmark of the Buhari/Idiagbon regime of 1984.

quiz.q: Which crisis is associated with 'Operation Wetie'?
quiz.solution: The violent aftermath of the rigged 1965 Western Region election was known as Operation Wetie.
Civil rule returned on 29 May 1999 with Olusegun Obasanjo's inauguration.

quiz.q: One major demerit of military rule is that it
quiz.solution: Military regimes routinely curtail civil liberties, ban parties and muzzle the press.
